chapter_text:
CHAPTER 22 - PRINCIPLES OF GENETICS

Introduction

Why do offspring resemble their parents and yet differ from them? Genetics is the branch of biology that studies HEREDITY (the transmission of characters from parents to offspring) and VARIATION (the differences among individuals). The foundations of modern genetics were laid by Gregor Johann Mendel, an Austrian monk, whose careful experiments on the garden pea (Pisum sativum) between 1856 and 1863 revealed the basic rules by which characters are inherited. This chapter develops Mendel's monohybrid and dihybrid crosses and the laws he deduced, then extends the story to incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, the chromosomal theory of inheritance, linkage and crossing over, sex determination, sex-linked inheritance, mutations and pedigree analysis.

22.1 MENDEL AND HIS WORK WITH THE GARDEN PEA

Mendel chose the garden pea for good reasons: it has several clear-cut contrasting characters, it is easy to grow, it has a short life cycle, it produces many seeds, and it is normally SELF-POLLINATING (so pure lines are easy to maintain), yet it can be CROSS-POLLINATED by hand when required. Mendel worked with seven pairs of contrasting characters, for example seed shape (round vs wrinkled), seed colour (yellow vs green), flower colour (violet vs white), pod shape, pod colour, flower position and stem height (tall vs dwarf). Before crossing, he raised PURE-BREEDING (true-breeding) lines that produced only one form of a character generation after generation. His success came from counting large numbers of offspring and analysing the results mathematically - a novel approach for his time.

Some key terms:
- GENE: the unit of heredity that controls a character; a segment of DNA on a chromosome.
- ALLELE: one of the alternative forms of a gene (for example T for tall and t for dwarf).
- DOMINANT: the allele that expresses itself in the heterozygote and masks the other (written as a capital letter, e.g. T).
- RECESSIVE: the allele that is masked in the heterozygote and expresses only when present in a double dose (written as a small letter, e.g. t).
- HOMOZYGOUS: having two identical alleles for a character (TT or tt); also called pure.
- HETEROZYGOUS: having two different alleles for a character (Tt); also called hybrid.
- GENOTYPE: the genetic make-up of an individual (TT, Tt or tt).
- PHENOTYPE: the observable character or appearance (tall or dwarf).
- F1 GENERATION: the first filial generation, the offspring of the parental (P) cross.
- F2 GENERATION: the second filial generation, obtained by self-pollinating or interbreeding the F1.

22.2 MONOHYBRID CROSS

A MONOHYBRID CROSS follows the inheritance of a SINGLE pair of contrasting characters. Mendel crossed a pure tall pea plant (TT) with a pure dwarf plant (tt). All the F1 plants were TALL (Tt) - the dwarf character had disappeared. When he allowed the F1 plants to self-pollinate, the dwarf character REAPPEARED in the F2 generation, in a definite ratio of about 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

The cross can be shown as:

   P:        TT (tall)   x   tt (dwarf)
   Gametes:    T                t
   F1:            Tt (all tall)

Selfing the F1 (Tt x Tt), the gametes T and t from each parent combine. A PUNNETT SQUARE shows the results:

              T          t
         +----------+----------+
      T  |   TT     |   Tt     |
         +----------+----------+
      t  |   Tt     |   tt     |
         +----------+----------+

F2 genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt (genotypic ratio 1:2:1).
F2 phenotypes: 3 tall : 1 dwarf (phenotypic ratio 3:1).

The tall F2 plants are of two kinds - one-third are pure (TT) and two-thirds are hybrid (Tt) - but all look alike because T is dominant.

22.3 MENDEL'S LAWS OF INHERITANCE

From the monohybrid cross Mendel deduced two laws.

LAW OF DOMINANCE: In a heterozygote, one allele (the dominant) expresses itself and masks the effect of the other (the recessive). This explains why all F1 plants are tall even though they carry the dwarf allele. Characters are controlled by discrete units (factors, now called genes) that occur in pairs; one of the pair is dominant over the other.

LAW OF SEGREGATION (Law of Purity of Gametes): The two alleles of a pair SEPARATE (segregate) during the formation of gametes, so that each gamete receives only ONE allele of the pair. The alleles do not blend or contaminate each other; they remain pure. When gametes fuse at fertilisation, the paired condition is restored. This is why the recessive dwarf character, hidden in the F1, reappears unchanged in the F2. The law of segregation has no exceptions and is universally true.

TEST CROSS: A tall plant may be TT or Tt - its genotype cannot be told from its appearance. To find out, it is crossed with a HOMOZYGOUS RECESSIVE (dwarf, tt). This is a test cross.
- If the tall plant is TT: TT x tt gives all Tt (all tall).
- If the tall plant is Tt: Tt x tt gives 1 Tt : 1 tt, i.e. 1 tall : 1 dwarf.
So a 1:1 ratio in the offspring reveals a heterozygous parent, while all-tall offspring reveal a homozygous parent. A test cross is a valuable tool for determining an unknown genotype. A cross between two F1 heterozygotes (Tt x Tt) is a BACK CROSS only loosely; strictly a back cross is a cross of the F1 with either parent.

22.4 DIHYBRID CROSS AND THE LAW OF INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT

A DIHYBRID CROSS follows TWO pairs of contrasting characters at the same time. Mendel crossed a pure plant with round yellow seeds (RRYY) and one with wrinkled green seeds (rryy). Round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r), and yellow (Y) over green (y).

   P:      RRYY (round yellow)  x  rryy (wrinkled green)
   Gametes:      RY                       ry
   F1:               RrYy (all round yellow)

The F1 plants produce FOUR kinds of gametes in equal numbers: RY, Ry, rY and ry, because the two gene pairs assort independently. Selfing the F1 (RrYy x RrYy) and combining the sixteen boxes of the Punnett square gives a phenotypic ratio of

   9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green (9:3:3:1)

Note that two NEW combinations appear - round green and wrinkled yellow - that were not present in the parents. From these results Mendel framed the

LAW OF INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT: When two or more pairs of characters are considered together, the alleles of one pair assort (segregate) INDEPENDENTLY of the alleles of the other pair during gamete formation. Each pair behaves as if the other were not present, so all possible combinations of characters are produced. The 9:3:3:1 ratio is simply the product of two independent 3:1 ratios: (3:1) x (3:1). This law holds only for genes on DIFFERENT chromosomes (or far apart on the same chromosome); linked genes are an exception.

22.5 INCOMPLETE DOMINANCE

In some crosses neither allele is completely dominant, and the heterozygote shows an INTERMEDIATE phenotype. This is INCOMPLETE DOMINANCE. In the four o'clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa) and in snapdragon (Antirrhinum), a cross between a red-flowered plant (RR) and a white-flowered plant (rr) gives F1 plants with PINK flowers (Rr). When the pink F1 are selfed, the F2 appears in the ratio 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white - a phenotypic ratio of 1:2:1, which is exactly the same as the genotypic ratio. Here the phenotype directly reveals the genotype, because the heterozygote is distinguishable from both homozygotes. The law of segregation still holds; only the law of dominance is modified.

22.6 CODOMINANCE AND MULTIPLE ALLELES

In CODOMINANCE both alleles express themselves FULLY and independently in the heterozygote, so both characters appear together (not a blend). The best example is the human ABO blood group system. The gene I has three alleles: I-A, I-B and i. I-A and I-B are codominant with each other, while both are dominant over i.
- Genotype I-A I-A or I-A i gives blood group A.
- Genotype I-B I-B or I-B i gives blood group B.
- Genotype I-A I-B gives blood group AB (both antigens A and B are present - codominance).
- Genotype ii gives blood group O.
Because a single gene has more than two allelic forms in the population (here three), this is also an example of MULTIPLE ALLELES. Any one individual carries only two of the alleles, but the population as a whole has more than two. Multiple alleles arise by repeated mutation of the same gene. The ABO system gives four phenotypes (A, B, AB, O) from three alleles.

22.7 THE CHROMOSOMAL THEORY OF INHERITANCE

Mendel's factors were abstract until chromosomes were seen to behave in exactly the same way during meiosis. Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri (around 1902) proposed the CHROMOSOMAL THEORY OF INHERITANCE: genes are located on chromosomes, and it is the chromosomes that segregate and assort during meiosis, carrying the genes with them. The parallel is striking - chromosomes occur in pairs (homologous pairs) just as alleles do; the members of a pair separate during meiosis (like segregation); and different pairs assort independently (like independent assortment). Fertilisation restores the paired condition. Thus the physical behaviour of chromosomes provides the mechanism for Mendel's laws.

22.8 LINKAGE AND CROSSING OVER

If genes are on chromosomes, and each chromosome carries many genes, then genes on the SAME chromosome should tend to be inherited TOGETHER. This is LINKAGE. Thomas Hunt Morgan, working with the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, confirmed linkage in the early 1900s. Linked genes do not show independent assortment; they tend to stay in their parental combinations.

However, linkage is not absolute. During meiosis, homologous chromosomes exchange segments at points called chiasmata - a process called CROSSING OVER. Crossing over produces RECOMBINANT gametes with new combinations of alleles. The FREQUENCY of crossing over between two genes depends on the DISTANCE between them: the farther apart two genes are on a chromosome, the more often crossing over occurs between them, and the higher the recombination frequency. Morgan and his student Sturtevant used recombination frequencies to construct the first GENETIC MAPS (linkage maps), on which distances are measured in map units (one map unit = 1 percent recombination). Linkage and crossing over are therefore exceptions to, and extensions of, the law of independent assortment.

22.9 SEX DETERMINATION

The sex of an organism is usually decided by a special pair of chromosomes called SEX CHROMOSOMES (or allosomes); the remaining chromosomes are AUTOSOMES. Several mechanisms exist:

XX-XY type (humans, Drosophila): Females are XX (homogametic - all eggs carry an X). Males are XY (heterogametic - half the sperm carry X and half carry Y). The sex of the child is therefore determined by the FATHER'S sperm: an X-bearing sperm gives a girl (XX) and a Y-bearing sperm gives a boy (XY). The expected ratio is 1 male : 1 female. In humans there are 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes (46 chromosomes in all).

XX-XO type (many insects such as grasshoppers and bugs): Females are XX; males have a single X and no Y (written XO). Here again the male is heterogametic - some sperm carry X and some carry no sex chromosome.

ZZ-ZW type (birds, some reptiles, moths and butterflies): The situation is reversed. The MALE is homogametic (ZZ) and the FEMALE is heterogametic (ZW). The female's egg decides the sex of the offspring. The letters Z and W are used instead of X and Y to stress this reversal.

22.10 SEX-LINKED INHERITANCE

Genes located on the sex chromosomes (usually the X chromosome) show SEX-LINKED INHERITANCE. Because a male has only one X chromosome, a recessive allele on his X is expressed even in a single dose (the Y carries no corresponding allele). Such recessive X-linked conditions are therefore much commoner in males than in females. Two classic human examples:

HAEMOPHILIA: a recessive X-linked disorder in which the blood fails to clot properly, so even a small injury may cause prolonged bleeding. A carrier woman (one normal and one defective X) is healthy but passes the defective X to half her sons, who then have the disease. Haemophilia famously ran through several European royal families descending from Queen Victoria.

COLOUR BLINDNESS (red-green): a recessive X-linked condition in which a person cannot distinguish red from green. A colour-blind man crossed with a carrier woman can produce colour-blind daughters, but usually a colour-blind man's daughters are carriers. About 8 percent of men but under 1 percent of women are red-green colour blind, reflecting the single-X situation in males.

22.11 MUTATIONS

A MUTATION is a sudden, heritable change in the genetic material. Mutations are the ultimate source of new variation and hence the raw material of evolution.
- GENE (point) MUTATIONS involve a change in a single gene, for example the substitution, addition or deletion of a base in the DNA. Sickle-cell anaemia results from a single base change in the gene for haemoglobin.
- CHROMOSOMAL MUTATIONS (aberrations) involve changes in chromosome STRUCTURE (deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation) or in chromosome NUMBER. A change in number may be aneuploidy (one extra or missing chromosome, as in Down syndrome, trisomy of chromosome 21) or polyploidy (whole extra sets, common in plants).
Agents that increase the mutation rate - such as X-rays, ultraviolet light and certain chemicals - are called MUTAGENS.

22.12 PEDIGREE ANALYSIS

A PEDIGREE (family tree) is a chart showing the inheritance of a character through several generations of a family. By convention, males are shown as squares and females as circles; a horizontal line joins a mating pair, and affected individuals are shaded. Pedigree analysis lets geneticists trace whether a trait is dominant or recessive, and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked, and to estimate the risk that future children will be affected. It is an important tool in human genetics and genetic counselling, where family experiments (controlled crosses) are impossible.

SUMMARY

- Genetics studies heredity and variation. Mendel used the garden pea, chose contrasting characters, raised pure lines, and counted offspring.
- Key terms: gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype, F1, F2.
- Monohybrid cross (Tt x Tt): F2 phenotypic ratio 3:1 and genotypic ratio 1:2:1. A Punnett square predicts the outcome.
- Law of dominance: the dominant allele masks the recessive in the heterozygote. Law of segregation: the two alleles separate during gamete formation, each gamete getting one (gametes are pure).
- Test cross (unknown x homozygous recessive) reveals a genotype: all-dominant offspring means homozygous; a 1:1 ratio means heterozygous.
- Dihybrid cross (RrYy x RrYy): F2 phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1. Law of independent assortment: alleles of different gene pairs assort independently (for genes on different chromosomes).
- Incomplete dominance: heterozygote is intermediate (red x white gives pink; F2 = 1:2:1, phenotype = genotype). Codominance: both alleles express fully (ABO blood groups; AB genotype).
- Multiple alleles: a gene with more than two alleles in the population (I-A, I-B, i give A, B, AB, O).
- Chromosomal theory (Sutton and Boveri): genes lie on chromosomes, whose meiotic behaviour explains segregation and independent assortment.
- Linkage (Morgan, Drosophila): genes on the same chromosome are inherited together; crossing over produces recombinants, more frequent for genes farther apart (basis of genetic maps).
- Sex determination: XX-XY (humans, male heterogametic), XX-XO (many insects), ZZ-ZW (birds, female heterogametic). In humans the father's sperm decides the sex.
- Sex-linked inheritance: X-linked recessive traits (haemophilia, red-green colour blindness) are commoner in males because they have a single X.
- Mutations (gene and chromosomal) are sudden heritable changes and the source of new variation; mutagens increase their rate. Pedigree analysis traces inheritance in human families.

topics.name: Mendel and Monohybrid Cross
topics.description: Gregor Mendel's choice of the garden pea and contrasting characters; key terms (gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype, F1, F2); the monohybrid cross giving the 3:1 phenotypic and 1:2:1 genotypic ratio in the F2; the Punnett square.

topics.name: Laws of Inheritance
topics.description: Mendel's law of dominance and law of segregation (purity of gametes) deduced from the monohybrid cross, and the test cross used to determine an unknown genotype (1:1 ratio reveals a heterozygote).

topics.name: Dihybrid Cross and Independent Assortment
topics.description: The dihybrid cross (RrYy x RrYy) giving the 9:3:3:1 F2 phenotypic ratio, the four kinds of gametes and new combinations, and Mendel's law of independent assortment for genes on different chromosomes.

topics.name: Incomplete Dominance, Codominance and Multiple Alleles
topics.description: Incomplete dominance (red x white gives pink in Mirabilis/snapdragon, F2 = 1:2:1), codominance (ABO blood groups, AB genotype) and multiple alleles (I-A, I-B, i giving four blood-group phenotypes).

topics.name: Linkage, Crossing Over and Chromosomal Theory
topics.description: The chromosomal theory of inheritance (Sutton and Boveri); linkage of genes on the same chromosome (Morgan, Drosophila); crossing over producing recombinants and the basis of genetic maps as exceptions to independent assortment.

topics.name: Sex Determination and Sex-Linked Inheritance
topics.description: Sex-determination mechanisms (XX-XY, XX-XO, ZZ-ZW), the role of the father's sperm in humans, sex-linked inheritance of X-linked recessives (haemophilia, colour blindness), mutations and pedigree analysis.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain why Mendel chose the garden pea and define the key genetic terms - gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype, F1 and F2.
Work out a monohybrid cross using a Punnett square and predict the 3:1 phenotypic and 1:2:1 genotypic ratios of the F2 generation.
State and explain Mendel's law of dominance and law of segregation, and use a test cross to determine an unknown genotype.
Perform a dihybrid cross, obtain the 9:3:3:1 F2 ratio, and state the law of independent assortment for genes on different chromosomes.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Incomplete Dominance, Codominance and Multiple Alleles
learning_outcomes.description: Distinguish incomplete dominance, codominance and multiple alleles, using Mirabilis flower colour (1:2:1) and the human ABO blood group system as examples.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Linkage, Crossing Over and Chromosomal Theory
learning_outcomes.description: Analyse the chromosomal theory of inheritance and explain linkage and crossing over (Morgan's work on Drosophila) as extensions of and exceptions to independent assortment.
Describe the XX-XY, XX-XO and ZZ-ZW mechanisms of sex determination and explain how sex is decided in humans, together with the nature of mutations and pedigree analysis.
Apply the pattern of X-linked recessive inheritance (haemophilia, colour blindness) to predict the ratios of affected and carrier offspring in a cross or pedigree.

chapter_summary.title: Principles of Genetics - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Biology (314) summary for Principles of Genetics. It develops Mendel's monohybrid and dihybrid crosses and his laws, then incomplete dominance and codominance, multiple alleles, the chromosomal theory, linkage and crossing over, sex determination and sex-linked inheritance, mutations and pedigree analysis.

sections.heading: Mendel and the monohybrid cross
bullets: Mendel used the self-pollinating garden pea with seven pairs of clear contrasting characters and raised pure-breeding lines.
A monohybrid cross (TT x tt) gives an all-tall F1 (Tt); selfing gives an F2 of 3 tall : 1 dwarf (genotype 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt).
Genotype is the genetic make-up; phenotype is the appearance; the dominant allele is written in capitals, the recessive in small letters.
A Punnett square is used to predict the kinds and proportions of offspring.

sections.heading: Mendel's laws of inheritance
bullets: Law of dominance: in a heterozygote the dominant allele expresses and masks the recessive.
Law of segregation: the two alleles of a pair separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one (gametes are pure).
A test cross (unknown x homozygous recessive) determines an unknown genotype.
All-dominant offspring means the tested parent was homozygous; a 1:1 ratio means it was heterozygous.

sections.heading: Dihybrid cross and independent assortment
bullets: A dihybrid cross (RrYy x RrYy) gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 9:3:3:1.
The F1 produces four kinds of gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in equal numbers.
New combinations (round green, wrinkled yellow) appear that were absent in the parents.
Law of independent assortment: alleles of different gene pairs assort independently, for genes on different chromosomes.

sections.heading: Beyond simple dominance
bullets: Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is intermediate - red x white gives pink; F2 = 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white (phenotype = genotype).
Codominance: both alleles express fully - the AB blood group shows both A and B antigens.
Multiple alleles: the ABO gene has three alleles (I-A, I-B, i) giving four phenotypes A, B, AB and O.
Any individual carries only two of the multiple alleles, though the population has more than two.

sections.heading: Chromosomes, linkage and sex
bullets: Chromosomal theory (Sutton and Boveri): genes lie on chromosomes whose meiotic behaviour explains Mendel's laws.
Linkage: genes on the same chromosome are inherited together (Morgan, Drosophila); crossing over produces recombinants, more often for genes farther apart.
Sex determination: XX-XY (humans, male heterogametic), XX-XO (many insects), ZZ-ZW (birds, female heterogametic); in humans the father's sperm decides sex.
X-linked recessives (haemophilia, red-green colour blindness) are commoner in males; mutations are heritable changes and pedigrees trace inheritance.

key_takeaways: Mendel's monohybrid cross gives an F2 of 3:1 (phenotype) and 1:2:1 (genotype); the dihybrid cross gives 9:3:3:1.
Law of dominance, law of segregation and law of independent assortment summarise Mendelian inheritance; a test cross reveals an unknown genotype.
Incomplete dominance gives an intermediate heterozygote (pink; F2 = 1:2:1); codominance shows both alleles fully (blood group AB).
Multiple alleles (I-A, I-B, i) give four ABO phenotypes, though each person carries only two alleles.
The chromosomal theory places genes on chromosomes; linkage and crossing over (Morgan) extend and limit independent assortment.
Sex is determined by XX-XY, XX-XO or ZZ-ZW systems; in humans the Y-bearing sperm gives a boy and the X-bearing sperm a girl.
X-linked recessive traits such as haemophilia and colour blindness are far commoner in males because males have a single X chromosome.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Principles of Genetics (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. For genetics problems, show the parental genotypes, gametes and a Punnett square where asked, and state the ratios clearly.

questions.question: Why did Mendel choose the garden pea (Pisum sativum) for his breeding experiments? Give any three reasons.
questions.answer: Mendel chose the garden pea because: (1) it has several clear-cut contrasting characters (e.g. tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds); (2) it is easy to grow, has a short life cycle and produces many seeds, so large numbers of offspring can be counted; (3) it is normally self-pollinating, so pure-breeding lines are easy to maintain, yet it can be cross-pollinated by hand when a controlled cross is needed.
questions.explanation: Contrasting characters, easy to grow, self- and cross-pollination.

questions.question: Define the terms genotype, phenotype, homozygous and heterozygous with one example each.
questions.answer: Genotype is the genetic make-up of an individual, e.g. Tt. Phenotype is the observable character or appearance, e.g. tall. Homozygous means having two identical alleles for a character (e.g. TT or tt) - pure-breeding. Heterozygous means having two different alleles for a character (e.g. Tt) - a hybrid.

questions.question: A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf plant (tt). Using a Punnett square, work out the F1 and F2 generations and state the phenotypic and genotypic ratios in the F2.
questions.answer:
P: TT (tall) x tt (dwarf). Gametes: T and t. F1: all Tt (tall) - the dwarf character disappears (law of dominance).

Selfing F1: Tt x Tt. Gametes T, t from each parent.

Punnett square:
         T        t
    T   TT       Tt
    t   Tt       tt

F2 genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so the genotypic ratio is 1:2:1.
F2 phenotypes: 3 tall : 1 dwarf, so the phenotypic ratio is 3:1.
The dwarf character reappears in the F2 because the alleles segregate unchanged (law of segregation).
questions.explanation: F1 all Tt; F2 = 3:1 phenotype, 1:2:1 genotype via Punnett square.

questions.question: State Mendel's law of segregation and explain why it is also called the law of purity of gametes.
questions.answer: Law of segregation: the two alleles of a pair separate (segregate) during the formation of gametes, so that each gamete receives only one allele of the pair; the paired condition is restored at fertilisation. It is called the law of purity of gametes because the two alleles do not blend or contaminate one another - each gamete carries a pure (single) allele, which is why a recessive character hidden in the F1 reappears unchanged in the F2.
questions.explanation: One allele per gamete; alleles stay pure, no blending.

questions.question: What is a test cross? A tall pea plant is test-crossed and the offspring are half tall and half dwarf. What was the genotype of the tall parent? Explain.
questions.answer: A test cross is a cross of an individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive individual to reveal the unknown genotype. Here the tall parent is crossed with a dwarf (tt). A 1 tall : 1 dwarf ratio (half and half) shows the tall parent was HETEROZYGOUS (Tt): Tt x tt gives 1 Tt (tall) : 1 tt (dwarf). Had the tall parent been TT, all offspring would have been tall.

questions.question: In a dihybrid cross a round-yellow seeded plant (RRYY) is crossed with a wrinkled-green seeded plant (rryy). Give the F1, the kinds of gametes formed by the F1, and the F2 phenotypic ratio. State the law illustrated.
questions.answer:
P: RRYY (round yellow) x rryy (wrinkled green). Gametes: RY and ry. F1: all RrYy (round yellow).

The F1 (RrYy) forms four kinds of gametes in equal numbers: RY, Ry, rY and ry, because the two gene pairs assort independently.

Selfing RrYy x RrYy gives the 16-box Punnett square with an F2 phenotypic ratio of
9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green (9:3:3:1).
New combinations (round green and wrinkled yellow) appear. This illustrates the LAW OF INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT - the alleles of one gene pair assort independently of the alleles of the other pair.
questions.explanation: F1 RrYy; 4 gamete types; 9:3:3:1; independent assortment.

questions.question: Distinguish between incomplete dominance and codominance, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote shows an INTERMEDIATE phenotype - neither allele is fully dominant. Example: in Mirabilis jalapa (four o'clock plant) red (RR) x white (rr) gives pink (Rr) flowers. In codominance BOTH alleles express fully and independently in the heterozygote, so both characters appear together. Example: the human AB blood group, where genotype I-A I-B produces both A and B antigens.
questions.explanation: Incomplete = blend/intermediate (pink); codominance = both fully shown (AB).

questions.question: Explain, with a cross, how a red-flowered and a white-flowered Mirabilis plant give an F2 ratio of 1:2:1.
questions.answer:
This is incomplete dominance. P: RR (red) x rr (white). F1: all Rr (pink) - intermediate. Selfing Rr x Rr:
         R        r
    R   RR       Rr
    r   Rr       rr
F2: 1 RR (red) : 2 Rr (pink) : 1 rr (white), a phenotypic ratio of 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Because the heterozygote (pink) is distinguishable from both homozygotes, the phenotypic ratio (1:2:1) equals the genotypic ratio.
questions.explanation: Rr is pink; F2 phenotype = genotype = 1:2:1.

questions.question: What is linkage? How does crossing over affect linked genes?
questions.answer: Linkage is the tendency of genes located on the SAME chromosome to be inherited together, because they cannot assort independently. Thomas Hunt Morgan demonstrated linkage in Drosophila. Crossing over is the exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes during meiosis; it breaks the parental combinations of linked genes and produces RECOMBINANT gametes with new allele combinations. The farther apart two genes are on a chromosome, the more often crossing over occurs between them, so the higher the recombination frequency - a fact used to construct genetic maps.
questions.explanation: Linkage = genes together on one chromosome; crossing over gives recombinants.

questions.question: Explain how sex is determined in humans (XX-XY system) and why haemophilia is far commoner in men than in women.
questions.answer:
In humans females are XX (homogametic - all eggs carry an X) and males are XY (heterogametic - half the sperm carry X, half carry Y). At fertilisation an X-bearing sperm gives a girl (XX) and a Y-bearing sperm gives a boy (XY); the sex of the child is therefore decided by the FATHER'S sperm, in an expected ratio of 1 male : 1 female.

Haemophilia is a recessive X-linked disorder. A male has only one X chromosome, so a single defective allele on his X is expressed (the Y carries no corresponding normal allele) and he is affected. A female has two X chromosomes, so she is affected only if BOTH carry the defective allele; with one defective and one normal X she is a healthy carrier. Because a male needs only one defective allele while a female needs two, haemophilia (and other X-linked recessives) is far commoner in men.
questions.explanation: Father's sperm decides sex; single X in males explains higher male frequency.

The genetic make-up of an organism is called its ________.
An organism with the genotype Tt is described as ________ for that character.
The scientific name of the garden pea used by Mendel is Pisum ________.
The F2 genotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross is ________.
A ________ square is used to predict the offspring of a genetic cross.
Mendel's law of ________ states that the two alleles of a pair separate during gamete formation.
In a test cross a 1:1 ratio of offspring shows the tested parent is ________.
The F2 phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross is ________.
An RrYy plant forms ________ kinds of gametes.
In snapdragon, red x white flowers give ________ flowers in the F1.
The blood group produced by the genotype I-A I-B is group ________.
Genes located on the same chromosome and inherited together show ________.
The exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes is called ________ ________.
In humans the sex of a child is decided by the ________ sperm.
questions.explanation: Father's sperm (X or Y) decides sex.

questions.question: Haemophilia is a recessive ________-linked disorder of blood clotting.
List any four reasons why Mendel selected the garden pea for his experiments.
questions.answer: Mendel selected the garden pea because: (1) it shows several pairs of clear contrasting characters; (2) it is easy to grow and has a short life cycle; (3) it produces many seeds, allowing large numbers to be counted; (4) it is normally self-pollinating (so pure lines are easily kept) but can be cross-pollinated by hand when required.

questions.question: Distinguish between a dominant and a recessive allele.
questions.answer: A dominant allele expresses its effect and masks the other allele in the heterozygote; it is written as a capital letter (e.g. T). A recessive allele is masked in the heterozygote and expresses only when present in a double dose (homozygous); it is written as a small letter (e.g. t).
questions.explanation: Dominant masks; recessive shows only when homozygous.

questions.question: What are the F1 and F2 generations?
questions.answer: The F1 (first filial) generation is the offspring produced by crossing the parental (P) plants. The F2 (second filial) generation is obtained by self-pollinating or interbreeding the F1 individuals.
questions.explanation: F1 = offspring of P; F2 = offspring of F1.

questions.question: A monohybrid cross gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf in the F2. Write the genotypes of the F2 tall plants and their proportions.
questions.answer: The tall F2 plants are of two genotypes: pure tall TT and hybrid tall Tt. Of the three tall plants, one is TT and two are Tt, i.e. the tall plants are in the ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt. All look alike because T is dominant over t.

questions.question: Using a Punnett square, show a cross between two heterozygous violet-flowered pea plants (Vv) and give the F2 ratio.
questions.answer:
Vv x Vv. Gametes V and v.
        V       v
   V   VV      Vv
   v   Vv      vv
Offspring: 1 VV : 2 Vv : 1 vv = 3 violet : 1 white. Phenotypic ratio 3:1, genotypic ratio 1:2:1.

questions.question: A tall pea plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a dwarf plant and all offspring are tall. What was the genotype of the tall plant? Give reasons.
questions.answer: The tall plant was homozygous dominant (TT). In a test cross with a dwarf (tt), TT x tt gives all Tt (tall). Had it been heterozygous (Tt), the cross Tt x tt would have given a 1 tall : 1 dwarf ratio. Since all offspring are tall, the parent must be TT.

questions.question: State Mendel's law of dominance.
questions.answer: Law of dominance: characters are controlled by discrete units (factors, now genes) that occur in pairs. When a pair has two contrasting alleles, one (the dominant) expresses itself and masks the effect of the other (the recessive) in the heterozygote. This is why all F1 individuals of a monohybrid cross resemble one parent.
questions.explanation: Dominant allele masks recessive in heterozygote.

questions.question: Why is the law of segregation considered universally true and without exception?
questions.answer: The law of segregation depends only on the separation of homologous chromosomes (and hence the alleles they carry) during meiosis, which happens in every sexually reproducing organism. Each gamete therefore always receives just one allele of a pair, and the alleles remain pure and unaltered. Because this behaviour is a direct result of meiosis, no exceptions to the law of segregation are known.
questions.explanation: Follows directly from meiosis; no exceptions.

questions.question: State Mendel's law of independent assortment.
questions.answer: Law of independent assortment: when two or more pairs of contrasting characters are considered together, the alleles of one pair assort (segregate) independently of the alleles of the other pair during gamete formation. As a result all possible combinations of characters are produced, giving the 9:3:3:1 ratio in the dihybrid F2. The law applies to genes on different chromosomes.
questions.explanation: Alleles of different pairs assort independently.

questions.question: Explain how the 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio can be seen as the product of two 3:1 ratios.
questions.answer: In a dihybrid cross each character pair on its own segregates in a 3:1 ratio (3 dominant : 1 recessive). Because the two pairs assort independently, their outcomes multiply: (3:1) for the first character combined with (3:1) for the second gives 9 (both dominant) : 3 (first dominant, second recessive) : 3 (first recessive, second dominant) : 1 (both recessive), i.e. 9:3:3:1.

questions.question: List the four kinds of gametes produced by an RrYy plant and explain why four kinds are formed.
questions.answer: The four gametes are RY, Ry, rY and ry, formed in equal numbers. Four kinds arise because the two gene pairs (R/r and Y/y) assort independently during meiosis: each gamete gets one allele of each pair, and every combination of the two pairs is equally likely.
questions.explanation: RY, Ry, rY, ry by independent assortment.

questions.question: What is incomplete dominance? Give the F2 ratio and one example.
questions.answer: Incomplete dominance is inheritance in which neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype. Example: in Mirabilis jalapa (four o'clock plant) or snapdragon, red (RR) x white (rr) gives pink (Rr) F1. On selfing, the F2 appears as 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, a phenotypic ratio of 1:2:1 (equal to the genotypic ratio).

questions.question: Explain codominance using the human ABO blood group system.
questions.answer: Codominance is inheritance in which both alleles express themselves fully and independently in the heterozygote. In the ABO system the alleles I-A and I-B are codominant. A person of genotype I-A I-B has blood group AB and produces BOTH the A and the B antigens on the red cells - not a blend of the two. Both I-A and I-B are dominant over the allele i (group O).
questions.explanation: AB shows both A and B antigens fully.

questions.question: What are multiple alleles? Illustrate with the ABO blood groups.
questions.answer: Multiple alleles are three or more alternative forms of the same gene present in a population (though any one individual carries only two). The ABO gene has three alleles - I-A, I-B and i. Their combinations give four phenotypes: I-A I-A or I-A i (group A), I-B I-B or I-B i (group B), I-A I-B (group AB) and ii (group O).
questions.explanation: Three alleles I-A, I-B, i give four groups.

questions.question: What is the chromosomal theory of inheritance? Name the scientists who proposed it.
questions.answer: The chromosomal theory of inheritance (proposed by Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri around 1902) states that genes are located on chromosomes, and that it is the chromosomes which segregate and assort independently during meiosis, carrying the genes with them. The parallel behaviour of chromosomes and Mendel's factors provides the physical basis for his laws.
questions.explanation: Genes on chromosomes; Sutton and Boveri.

questions.question: Explain how the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis parallels Mendel's laws.
questions.answer: Chromosomes occur in homologous pairs, just as alleles occur in pairs. During meiosis the members of a homologous pair separate and pass into different gametes - this parallels the law of segregation. Different homologous pairs orient and separate independently of one another - this parallels the law of independent assortment. Fertilisation restores the paired condition. Thus chromosome behaviour provides the mechanism behind Mendel's laws.
questions.explanation: Pairing, separation and independent orientation mirror the laws.

questions.question: How did Morgan's work on Drosophila show that genes are linked?
questions.answer: Morgan crossed Drosophila differing in two characters whose genes lie on the same chromosome. Instead of the independent 9:3:3:1 assortment expected of unlinked genes, the parental combinations of characters stayed together far more often than recombinants. This tendency of certain genes to be inherited together showed that they are linked on the same chromosome, and the recombinants that did appear were explained by crossing over.

questions.question: Describe the XX-XY mechanism of sex determination in humans.
questions.answer: In humans, cells have 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Females are XX (homogametic) - every egg carries an X. Males are XY (heterogametic) - half the sperm carry X and half carry Y. If an X-bearing sperm fertilises the egg, the child is a girl (XX); if a Y-bearing sperm does, the child is a boy (XY). The expected sex ratio is 1 male : 1 female, and the sex of the child is decided by the father's sperm.
questions.explanation: Female XX, male XY; father's sperm decides sex.

questions.question: Distinguish between the XX-XO and ZZ-ZW mechanisms of sex determination.
questions.answer: In the XX-XO system (many insects such as grasshoppers) the female is XX and the male has a single X with no Y (XO); the male is heterogametic and some sperm carry X while others carry no sex chromosome. In the ZZ-ZW system (birds, moths, butterflies) the situation is reversed: the male is homogametic (ZZ) and the female is heterogametic (ZW), so the egg decides the sex of the offspring.
questions.explanation: XX-XO male heterogametic; ZZ-ZW female heterogametic.

questions.question: Distinguish between a gene mutation and a chromosomal mutation, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: A gene (point) mutation is a change within a single gene, such as the substitution, addition or deletion of a base in DNA; e.g. sickle-cell anaemia from a single base change in the haemoglobin gene. A chromosomal mutation is a change in chromosome structure (deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation) or number (aneuploidy or polyploidy); e.g. Down syndrome from an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21).
questions.explanation: Gene = single gene change; chromosomal = structure/number change.

questions.question: Why are more men than women red-green colour blind?
questions.answer: Red-green colour blindness is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A man has only one X chromosome, so a single copy of the defective allele is enough to make him colour blind (his Y carries no corresponding normal allele). A woman has two X chromosomes and is colour blind only if BOTH carry the defective allele; with one normal X she is a healthy carrier. Because a man needs only one defective allele while a woman needs two, colour blindness is much commoner in men.
questions.explanation: Single X in males => one recessive allele suffices.

questions.question: A colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous normal. Describe the colour vision of their sons and daughters.
questions.answer: Let X^c be the colour-blind allele. Father is X^c Y (colour blind); mother is X X (homozygous normal). Sons receive the Y from the father and one normal X from the mother (X X^? ... actually X from mother, Y from father): sons are X Y with the mother's normal X, so all sons have NORMAL colour vision. Daughters receive the father's X^c and the mother's normal X, so all daughters are X X^c - carriers with normal vision but able to pass the allele on. Thus no child is colour blind, but all daughters are carriers.

questions.question: Explain, with a labelled cross and a Punnett square, a monohybrid cross between a pure tall and a pure dwarf pea plant. State the ratios and the laws illustrated.
questions.answer:
P: TT (tall) x tt (dwarf). Gametes: T and t. F1: all Tt - tall, because T is dominant (law of dominance); the dwarf character disappears.

Selfing F1 (Tt x Tt), gametes T and t from each:
        T        t
   T   TT       Tt
   t   Tt       tt

F2 genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt (genotypic ratio 1:2:1).
F2 phenotypes: 3 tall : 1 dwarf (phenotypic ratio 3:1).
The dwarf character reappears because the alleles separate unchanged during gamete formation (law of segregation / purity of gametes). Thus the cross illustrates both the law of dominance (F1 all tall) and the law of segregation (dwarf returns in F2).
questions.explanation: Full monohybrid cross, 3:1 and 1:2:1, two laws.

questions.question: Describe a dihybrid cross and show how the 9:3:3:1 ratio arises. State the law of independent assortment.
questions.answer:
P: RRYY (round yellow) x rryy (wrinkled green). Gametes RY and ry. F1: all RrYy (round yellow).

The F1 (RrYy) forms four kinds of gametes in equal numbers - RY, Ry, rY, ry - because the two gene pairs assort independently. Selfing RrYy x RrYy gives a 16-box Punnett square. Combining the boxes:
- 9 round yellow (R_Y_)
- 3 round green (R_yy)
- 3 wrinkled yellow (rrY_)
- 1 wrinkled green (rryy)
So the F2 phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1. New combinations (round green, wrinkled yellow) appear that were absent in the parents.

Law of independent assortment: the alleles of one gene pair assort independently of the alleles of another pair during gamete formation, so every combination of characters is produced. This holds for genes on different chromosomes.
questions.explanation: Dihybrid cross, four gametes, 9:3:3:1, law stated.

questions.question: Compare incomplete dominance and codominance. For each, describe an example and give the F2 (or offspring) ratio.
questions.answer:
Both are departures from simple complete dominance, but they differ in how the heterozygote looks.

Incomplete dominance: neither allele is fully dominant, so the heterozygote is INTERMEDIATE. Example: in Mirabilis jalapa (or snapdragon), red (RR) x white (rr) gives pink (Rr) F1. Selfing gives F2 = 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white (1:2:1). The phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio because the heterozygote (pink) is distinct.

Codominance: both alleles express FULLY and independently, so both characters appear together (not blended). Example: the human ABO blood group - genotype I-A I-B gives group AB, with both A and B antigens present. A cross I-A i x I-B i gives offspring in the ratio 1 A : 1 B : 1 AB : 1 O (1:1:1:1).

Thus in incomplete dominance the heterozygote is a blend/intermediate, while in codominance both distinct characters are shown side by side.

questions.question: What are multiple alleles? Explain the inheritance of the ABO blood groups and list the possible genotypes of each group.
questions.answer:
Multiple alleles are three or more alternative forms of a single gene present in a population; any one individual carries only two of them. They arise by repeated mutation of the same gene.

The ABO blood group gene has three alleles: I-A, I-B and i. I-A and I-B are codominant with each other, and both are dominant over i. The genotypes and phenotypes are:
- Group A: I-A I-A or I-A i
- Group B: I-B I-B or I-B i
- Group AB: I-A I-B (codominance - both antigens present)
- Group O: ii
So three alleles produce four phenotypes (A, B, AB, O). This system combines multiple alleles (three forms of one gene) with codominance (in the AB group).
questions.explanation: Three alleles; genotypes of A, B, AB, O.

questions.question: Explain linkage and crossing over, and describe how they modify Mendel's law of independent assortment.
questions.answer:
Linkage is the tendency of genes located on the SAME chromosome to be inherited together, because they cannot assort independently. Morgan demonstrated linkage in Drosophila: linked genes stayed in their parental combinations far more often than expected under independent assortment, so linked genes are an EXCEPTION to that law.

Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding segments between homologous chromosomes at chiasmata during meiosis. It breaks parental combinations of linked genes and produces RECOMBINANT gametes with new allele combinations. The frequency of crossing over between two genes rises with the distance between them, so widely spaced genes recombine more often. Sturtevant used these recombination frequencies to build the first genetic (linkage) maps, measured in map units (1 map unit = 1% recombination).

Together, linkage limits independent assortment (genes on one chromosome tend to travel together), while crossing over partially restores new combinations - so the two processes both extend and qualify Mendel's third law.
questions.explanation: Linkage limits; crossing over restores combinations.

questions.question: Describe the three main mechanisms of sex determination (XX-XY, XX-XO, ZZ-ZW), naming an example organism for each.
questions.answer:
XX-XY type (humans, Drosophila): females are XX (homogametic), males are XY (heterogametic). Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y; the father's sperm decides the sex, giving an expected 1 male : 1 female ratio.

XX-XO type (many insects such as grasshoppers and bugs): females are XX; males have a single X and no Y (XO). The male is heterogametic - some sperm carry X, some carry no sex chromosome.

ZZ-ZW type (birds, some reptiles, moths and butterflies): the situation is reversed - the male is homogametic (ZZ) and the female is heterogametic (ZW). Here the female's egg decides the sex of the offspring; the letters Z and W stress this reversal.

In all three, sex is set by a special pair of sex chromosomes (allosomes) distinct from the autosomes.
questions.explanation: Three systems with examples and the heterogametic sex.

questions.question: Explain the inheritance of haemophilia. Using a cross, show the offspring of a carrier woman and a normal man.
questions.answer:
Haemophilia is a recessive X-linked disorder in which blood fails to clot properly. Let X^h be the haemophilia allele and X the normal allele.

A carrier woman is X X^h (healthy but carries the allele). A normal man is X Y.
Cross: X X^h (mother) x X Y (father).
         X            Y
   X    XX          XY
   X^h  X X^h       X^h Y

Offspring:
- Daughters: 1/2 XX (normal) and 1/2 X X^h (carrier) - none affected.
- Sons: 1/2 X Y (normal) and 1/2 X^h Y (haemophiliac).
So half the sons are expected to be haemophiliacs, half the daughters are carriers, and no daughter is affected. This explains why the disease usually passes from carrier mothers to sons.
questions.explanation: Carrier x normal: half sons affected, half daughters carriers.

questions.question: What is a pedigree? Explain how pedigree analysis is used in human genetics, and outline the standard symbols.
questions.answer:
A pedigree is a chart or family tree that shows the inheritance of a particular character through several generations of a family. Standard symbols are used: males are shown as squares and females as circles; a horizontal line joins a mating pair; vertical lines connect parents to their children; and affected individuals are shaded (unaffected are unshaded).

Because controlled breeding experiments are impossible in humans, geneticists study existing families instead. By examining a pedigree they can work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive, and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked (for example, an X-linked recessive trait affects mainly males and can skip generations through carrier females). Pedigree analysis is therefore central to genetic counselling, where it is used to estimate the risk that future children will inherit a disorder.
questions.explanation: Pedigree symbols and their use in tracing inheritance.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Gregor Mendel crossed a pure-breeding tall pea plant (TT) with a pure-breeding dwarf plant (tt). All the plants of the F1 generation were tall. When he allowed the F1 plants to self-pollinate, the F2 generation contained both tall and dwarf plants in a definite ratio.
(a) Give the genotype of the F1 plants.
(b) Why were all F1 plants tall?
(c) State the phenotypic and genotypic ratios of the F2.
(d) Which law explains the reappearance of the dwarf plants in the F2?
questions.answer:
(a) The F1 plants are all Tt (heterozygous tall).
(b) All F1 are tall because T (tall) is dominant over t (dwarf) and masks it in the heterozygote (law of dominance).
(c) F2 phenotypic ratio = 3 tall : 1 dwarf; F2 genotypic ratio = 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt (1:2:1).
(d) The law of segregation (purity of gametes) - the alleles separate unchanged into gametes, so the recessive dwarf allele reappears in the F2.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A farmer has a tall pea plant but does not know whether it is pure (TT) or hybrid (Tt). He wants to find out its genotype without waiting for many generations.
(a) Name the type of cross he should perform.
(b) With which plant should the tall plant be crossed?
(c) What result would show that the tall plant is heterozygous?
(d) What result would show that it is homozygous?
questions.answer:
(a) He should perform a test cross.
(b) The tall plant should be crossed with a homozygous recessive (dwarf, tt) plant.
(c) If the offspring appear in a ratio of 1 tall : 1 dwarf, the tall plant is heterozygous (Tt).
(d) If all the offspring are tall, the tall plant is homozygous dominant (TT).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a dihybrid cross, a pure round-yellow seeded pea plant (RRYY) was crossed with a pure wrinkled-green seeded plant (rryy). The F1 plants were all round and yellow. The F1 were then self-pollinated to raise the F2.
(a) Write the genotype and phenotype of the F1.
(b) How many kinds of gametes does the F1 produce, and name them.
(c) State the F2 phenotypic ratio.
(d) Name the two new combinations that appear in the F2.
questions.answer:
(a) The F1 genotype is RrYy and the phenotype is round yellow.
(b) The F1 produces four kinds of gametes: RY, Ry, rY and ry.
(c) The F2 phenotypic ratio is 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green (9:3:3:1).
(d) The two new (recombinant) combinations are round green and wrinkled yellow.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In the four o'clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa), a cross between a red-flowered plant and a white-flowered plant produces pink-flowered offspring. When these pink plants are self-pollinated, the next generation shows red, pink and white flowers.
(a) What name is given to this pattern of inheritance?
(b) Give the genotype of a pink plant.
(c) State the F2 ratio of red : pink : white.
(d) Why is the phenotypic ratio the same as the genotypic ratio here?
questions.answer:
(a) This is incomplete dominance.
(b) A pink plant is heterozygous, Rr.
(c) The F2 ratio is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white (1:2:1).
(d) Because the heterozygote (Rr) has its own distinct phenotype (pink), each genotype corresponds to a different phenotype, so the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Human ABO blood groups are controlled by a single gene with three alleles - I-A, I-B and i. I-A and I-B are codominant, and both are dominant over i. A man of blood group AB marries a woman of blood group O.
(a) Give the genotypes of the man and the woman.
(b) What blood groups can their children have?
(c) Which children, if any, can be of group AB or group O?
(d) What does this cross illustrate about codominance and multiple alleles?
questions.answer:
(a) The man (AB) is I-A I-B; the woman (O) is ii.
(b) The children can be group A (I-A i) or group B (I-B i), in a 1:1 ratio.
(c) None of the children can be group AB or group O - group AB needs both I-A and I-B (but each child gets i from the mother), and group O needs ii (but each child gets I-A or I-B from the father).
(d) It illustrates that a single gene can have multiple alleles (I-A, I-B, i) and that I-A and I-B are codominant, so the AB parent passes on either I-A or I-B, giving A or B children.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Thomas Hunt Morgan studied two genes located close together on the same chromosome of the fruit fly Drosophila. He found that the parental combinations of characters appeared far more often in the offspring than new combinations, though a few recombinants did occur.
(a) What is the phenomenon by which genes on the same chromosome are inherited together?
(b) What process produces the few recombinants?
(c) How does the distance between two genes affect the frequency of recombinants?
(d) What are recombination frequencies used to construct?
questions.answer:
(a) The phenomenon is linkage.
(b) The recombinants are produced by crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis.
(c) The greater the distance between two genes, the higher the frequency of crossing over and hence of recombinants; genes close together recombine rarely.
(d) Recombination frequencies are used to construct genetic (linkage) maps showing the order of and distances between genes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In humans, body cells contain 46 chromosomes - 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Females are XX and males are XY. A couple is expecting their first child.
(a) Which parent determines the sex of the child, and why?
(b) What is the expected ratio of boys to girls?
(c) Which sex is described as heterogametic and why?
(d) Name one animal group in which the female, not the male, is heterogametic.
questions.answer:
(a) The father determines the sex, because he is XY and produces two kinds of sperm (X-bearing and Y-bearing); an X sperm gives a girl and a Y sperm gives a boy, while the mother's eggs all carry X.
(b) The expected ratio is 1 boy : 1 girl (1:1).
(c) The male is heterogametic because he produces two different kinds of gametes (X and Y).
(d) Birds (also moths and butterflies), which follow the ZZ-ZW system where the female is ZW.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Colour blindness (red-green) is a recessive X-linked trait. A woman who is a carrier for colour blindness marries a man with normal colour vision. Let X^c be the colour-blind allele.
(a) Write the genotypes of the woman and the man.
(b) What fraction of their sons is expected to be colour blind?
(c) What fraction of their daughters is expected to be colour blind?
(d) Explain why the daughters are not colour blind in this cross.
questions.answer:
(a) The carrier woman is X X^c; the normal man is X Y.
(b) Half (1/2) of the sons are expected to be colour blind (those receiving the X^c from the mother).
(c) None (0) of the daughters is colour blind.
(d) The daughters receive a normal X from the father; even the one carrying X^c from the mother also has the father's normal X, so the normal dominant allele masks the defect - such daughters are carriers, not colour blind.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A mutation is a sudden, heritable change in the genetic material. Mutations may involve a single gene or whole chromosomes, and certain agents increase the rate at which they occur.
(a) Name the two broad types of mutation.
(b) Give one example of a disorder caused by a gene mutation.
(c) Give one example of a disorder caused by a change in chromosome number.
(d) What name is given to agents such as X-rays and UV light that raise the mutation rate?
questions.answer:
(a) The two broad types are gene (point) mutations and chromosomal mutations (aberrations).
(b) Sickle-cell anaemia, caused by a single base change in the haemoglobin gene, is an example of a gene mutation.
(c) Down syndrome, caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), is an example of a change in chromosome number.
(d) Such agents are called mutagens.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A pedigree is a family tree that records the inheritance of a trait across generations. In one family, a certain disorder appears mainly in males and can pass from an unaffected mother to her sons.
(a) In a pedigree, how are males and females represented?
(b) How are affected individuals shown?
(c) The pattern described (mainly males, passed through unaffected mothers) suggests what kind of inheritance?
(d) Why is pedigree analysis, rather than experimental crosses, used in human genetics?
questions.answer:
(a) Males are shown as squares and females as circles.
(b) Affected individuals are shown shaded (filled in); unaffected individuals are unshaded.
(c) The pattern suggests X-linked recessive inheritance, as the trait appears mainly in males and is carried by unaffected (carrier) mothers.
(d) Because controlled breeding experiments cannot be performed on humans, geneticists must study the inheritance of traits in existing families through pedigree analysis, which is also used in genetic counselling.
